historical_record.description: The Art Commission approved the Phase 3 drawings for the multi-purpose building at Storyland, the zoo's children's area, by J. Francis Ward.
The Art Commission approved the Phase 3 drawings for the zoo's African Scene, whose first drawings by J. Francis Ward it had approved on March 1, 1965.
With $7,500 voted by the Board of Supervisors, the Recreation and Park Commission engaged J. Francis Ward, architect, to draw a master plan for the zoo.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded the contract to build Storyland, a children's attraction at Fleishhacker Playfield, to Hub Pacific Building Company of Menlo Park at $147,750.
The Recreation and Park Commission engaged the designer Donald G. Clever, for a fee of $19,115, to make the murals, figures and other features of Storyland at Fleishhacker Playfield.

The Recreation and Park Commission accepted the San Francisco Zoological Society's gift of plans and specifications by W. R. Spackman, architect, for an Orangutan Grotto to be built at the zoo, subject to the Department of Public Works' engineers.
The Recreation and Park Commission approved J. Francis Ward's plan for a Little Theater building, to be built in Storyland by the San Francisco Zoological Society.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved J. Francis Ward's plans for the African Scene at the zoo, already passed by the Art Commission, at an estimated $120,000, to be built by the San Francisco Zoological Society.
The Recreation and Park Commission approved Corlett and Spackman's plans for moating the axis deer area at the zoo.
The Recreation and Park Commission approved Corlett and Spackman's final plans for the Tropical Bird Aviary at the zoo.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded the $407,000 contract for a new animal hospital and alterations to the service building at the zoo to Mission Contractors Joint Venture.
The zoo's new animal hospital was formally dedicated just before the Recreation and Park Commission's meeting; the zoo's veterinarian, Dr. Mottram, had played a major part in its design.

The Recreation and Park Commission adopted in principle "A Plan for the San Francisco Zoo" by Esherick, Hornsey, Dodge and Davis, architects and planners, covering land use, landscaping, the collections, buildings and circulation, subject to environmental review of each project; Joseph Esherick had presented the preliminary plan in March.

The zoo's Musk Ox Meadow, a naturalistic exhibit built for over $250,000 in grant funds as the home of nine musk oxen, was dedicated on June 6, 1980, next to the new Gorilla World, which Mayor Dianne Feinstein was to dedicate on August 1.

After P. Steven Peris of Marquis Associates showed the schematic plans, with plantings to soften its large stucco facade, the Recreation and Park Commission approved the renovation of the zoo's Lion House.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the plans for the zoo's new Primate Discovery Center, on which $400,000 had already been spent in design; in October it approved funds from the Eskey Estate toward building it.
The Recreation and Park Commission renamed Zoo Road, leading to the zoo, Herbst Road, for the Herbst Foundation's help to the zoo and to the Recreation Center for the Handicapped.
The Recreation and Park Commission approved $60,689 from the Eskey Estate Fund to build the zoo's Koala Exhibit, designed by Linda Rhodes, architect, and named it in honor of Mae Bogert Eskey.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the schematic site plan for a mammal breeding and holding center for the zoo, part of its Zoo 2000 plan, on land shared with the Clean Water Program's southwest treatment plant.

The renovated Asian Elephant Exhibit at the Zoo was dedicated on January 10, 1991, with sand in the outdoor yard and heated floors in the night quarters, as the Zoo moved to a "hands off" way of managing its elephants.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved demolishing the Zoo's Monkey Island, completed in 1940 and among the first major monkey islands in the United States, whose poorly sealed rebar had left it failing, to make way for the South American Gateway exhibit.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the Zoological Society's South American Gateway, a 4-acre exhibit with an entry building of primates, tapirs, capybara, pudu, waterfowl and turtles, a strangler fig area, a 9,000-square-foot aviary and underwater viewing.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded Barnes/LTM, a joint venture, a $1,903,000 contract to build the Zoo's Avian Conservation Center.

The Board of Park Commissioners approved Lewis P. Hobart's general plans for extending the Zoo, to be built unit by unit as the Works Progress Administration found the money, in the order monkey island, flight cages, bear pit, lion and tiger house and bird cages, with Hobart paid six per cent of each unit for its detailed plans.
The Board of Park Commissioners approved the plans and specifications for the Lion House at Fleishhacker Zoo.

The architect Lewis P. Hobart brought the Board of Park Commissioners his drawings for the buffalo and gnu paddocks and barns at the Zoo, paid for through the Work Projects Administration's coordinating committee.
The Park Commission engaged Ward and Bolles, architects, to design the Primate House and the Panther and Leopard House at the Zoo and supervise their construction, for no more than $7,250.
